strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear visualization of fixed viewpoint occlusion limitations; practical relevance to robotic manipulation
Thoughtfully designed TaskMoE using instruction+visual routing and decoupled gating (N_G < N_J) for parameter sharing and generalization
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 18 RLBench tasks including ablation studies, sensitivity analysis, performance-efficiency trade-offs, and real-world validation
Solid empirical improvements (86.7% vs 84.9% average; 6.4% gain on occlusion tasks) with modest 10.7% inference overhead
Practical three-stage training strategy that leverages demonstration data without requiring online environment interaction
Clear presentation with informative architecture diagrams and logical exposition
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: MoE and view planning are established techniques; the primary contribution is their combination, which is reasonable but not substantially novel

Pseudo-environment mechanism under-justified: relegated to supplementary materials, uses frozen reference model for rewards without comparison to alternative designs, learnable weight components lack ablation

TaskMoE design choices lack empirical justification: N_G=8, N_E=16 appear arbitrary with no ablations; no visualization of discovered task clusters; no direct comparison of instruction+vision routing vs. task-ID-only routing

View planning policy overly simplistic: MLP predicting K poses in parallel without sequential planning; K=3 chosen without justification despite Table 3 showing improvements up to K=4; multi-component reward lacks ablation on relative importance
Limited real-world validation: only 5 tasks vs 18 in simulation; 100 demos per task; no quantitative baseline comparisons; success rates not clearly reported; transfer quality unclear
Statistical rigor concerns: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; unclear if results averaged over runs; single numbers in tables without variance estimates
Overstated generalization claims: zero-shot test on 'Open drawer' is semantically similar to training tasks; only one OOD task with 12% success rate; insufficient evidence of true generalization
Baseline comparisons outdated: only RVT2, ARP, ARP+ tested; no comparison with recent VLA methods (OpenVLA, RT-2, π0) mentioned in related work
Occlusion improvement claims unclear: text suggests 56% improvement but Table 1 shows 6.4% for put_in_cupboard; source of 56% not clearly stated

Missing ablations and analyses: no breakdown of Stage 2 vs Stage 3 contributions; point cloud quality/resolution sensitivity unexplored; expert activation patterns not visualized; computational cost breakdown absent

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: Fixed camera viewpoints do cause occlusions in robotic manipulation, effectively illustrated in Figure 1
Comprehensive simulation experiments: 18 RLBench tasks with ablation studies and sensitivity analysis demonstrate thorough empirical work
Solid technical integration: Conceptually sensible combination of active view planning and task-aware representation learning with well-designed three-stage training
Real-world validation attempt: Demonstrates commitment to practical applicability with experiments on Dobot Xtrainer platform
Pragmatic engineering: Pseudo-environment mechanism effectively avoids expensive physical environment interaction during policy optimization
weaknesses: Marginal performance improvement: Only +1.8 pp average gain (84.9%→86.7%) inadequately justifies added complexity and computational overhead; many tasks show minimal or no improvement

Critical ablation study flaw: TaskMoE contributes only ~0.88 pp improvement while MVEP alone causes catastrophic performance drop (→8.89%), revealing TaskMoE is non-essential and undermining the paper's core narrative

Limited technical novelty: MVEP is straightforward RL-based camera pose optimization; TaskMoE applies existing MoE techniques with minor modifications (cross-attention+FiLM, decoupled gates)—incremental over prior work
Insufficient real-world validation: Only 5 tasks without baseline comparisons, no quantitative results, and qualitative descriptions only; sim-to-real transfer challenges not addressed
Weak generalization evidence: Zero-shot generalization tested on single unseen task ('Open drawer') with 12% success—insufficient to support generalization claims; more unseen tasks required

Unfair experimental comparison: TAVP uses 4 fixed RGB-D views plus dynamic views while baselines use only 4 fixed views; additional visual information may drive improvements rather than algorithmic innovation

Pseudo-environment mechanism lacks justification: Reward design (Eq. 6-9) appears ad-hoc with manual weighting; no ablation on reward components or justification for optimality; simpler baselines not compared
Insufficient statistical rigor: Success rates without confidence intervals; only 25 evaluation episodes per task; no significance testing to determine if improvements are statistically meaningful
Unjustified hyperparameter choices: K=3 selected but Table 3 shows K=4 performs better (55.2% vs 49.6%); NG=8, NE=16, and top-2 expert selection lack justification or ablation
Inadequate computational overhead analysis: 10.7% inference latency increase may be problematic for real-time robotics; memory overhead of dual networks not discussed
Limited scope of comparison: Only compared against RVT2, ARP, ARP+; missing comparisons with active vision methods, other MoE approaches, and recent VLA models
Point cloud dependency acknowledged but dismissed: Reliance on accurate depth maps problematic for reflective/transparent objects common in real manipulation; no robustness evaluation to noisy depth
Incomplete ablations: No ablation on individual reward components (r0, r1, r2), training strategy stages, or architectural choices; limited sensitivity analysis

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies and demonstrates occlusion limitations of fixed-view systems in robotic manipulation through compelling visualization (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 18 RLBench tasks, real-world validation, thorough ablations, sensitivity analysis, and zero-shot generalization experiments provide convincing evidence
Strong performance on occlusion-prone tasks: Up to +56% improvement on target tasks demonstrates the method effectively addresses its core problem space
Technically sound approach: Pseudo-environment mechanism for efficient RL training, thoughtful camera parameterization, and multi-stage training strategy are well-engineered
Task-aware feature extraction: TaskMoE design with cross-modal guidance and decoupled gates shows novel contribution beyond standard MoE approaches
Real-world validation: Physical robot experiments strengthen claims beyond simulation-only results, demonstrating practical viability
Clear presentation: Well-written paper with effective figures and clear methodology descriptions
weaknesses: Modest average performance gains: Overall improvement of only 1.8% across 18 tasks (84.9% → 86.7%), with many tasks showing <5% gains, suggesting narrow applicability
Limited real-world evaluation: Only 5 real-world tasks with qualitative results; explicit success rates for real-world experiments are not reported, reducing confidence in practical applicability
Critical point cloud dependency: Acknowledged difficulty handling reflective/transparent objects severely limits real-world deployment where such materials are common; no robustness analysis provided
Insufficient theoretical justification for pseudo-environment reward: Why action prediction loss on current observation predicts optimal viewpoints is not rigorously explained; design appears ad-hoc
Arbitrary TaskMoE design choices: Number of gates (NG=8) and experts (NE=16) lack sensitivity analysis; task-gate assignment mechanism unclear; cross-attention vs. simpler alternatives not compared
Weak generalization evidence: Only one unseen task tested with 12% success vs. 49.6% in-domain, insufficient to support generalization claims
Suspicious baseline performance: Random viewpoint ablation achieving 8.89% raises questions about baseline implementation quality and proper tuning
Complex training procedure: Three-stage training (supervised → RL → fine-tuning) is intricate and may hinder reproducibility and practical adoption
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compared against dense fixed-view models; no comparison with other active view planning or multi-view manipulation methods
Computational overhead incompletely analyzed: 10.7% inference latency increase (42ms) may be significant for time-critical applications; memory and training costs not discussed

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear examples of fixed-view limitations (occlusion, incomplete scene understanding)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 18 RLBench tasks with thorough ablations, sensitivity analyses, and real-world validation
Exceptional performance gains on occlusion-prone tasks (+56% on some tasks like Insert Peg)
Solid real-world experiments showing 20 percentage point improvement over Diffusion Policy baseline (88% vs 68%)
Rigorous ablation studies clearly demonstrating MVEP's dominant contribution (8.89% with random viewpoints vs 86.67% with TAVP)
Good presentation quality with clear motivation figures, comprehensive pipeline diagrams, and well-organized structure
Strong reproducibility: code to be released, detailed hyperparameters in tables, implementation details in appendix
Proper statistical reporting with standard deviations in most results
weaknesses: Modest improvements on main RLBench benchmark (86.6% vs 84.9% for ARP+ = 1.7 points), often within reported standard deviations (±2-5%), making improvements not clearly statistically significant

Incremental technical novelty: TaskMoE primarily adds decoupled gating to existing MoE approaches (Paper [14] already used MoE for multi-task policies); MVEP is straightforward application of point cloud + MLP + reparameterization, not novel

Pseudo-environment training mechanism lacks rigor: (a) uses frozen reference model trained on fixed views to optimize dynamic-view policy (questionable fairness), (b) reward function is ad-hoc (r0 lacks justification, r1 uses entropy heuristic, r2 uses cosine distance without principled motivation), (c) no ablation on reward design or weight sensitivity
Weak generalization evidence: zero-shot generalization tested on only ONE unseen task achieving only 12% success, insufficient to support generalization claims

Critical unaddressed real-world limitation: acknowledged difficulty with reflective/transparent objects due to point cloud dependency, yet no robustness testing against point cloud noise or segmentation errors, severely limiting practical applicability

Limited real-world validation: only 5 tasks with 10 trials each; only compared against Diffusion Policy (not RVT2/ARP variants); heavy occlusion remains challenging; all experiments on single-arm tabletop tasks

TaskMoE design not well justified: task-to-gate assignments appear manually designed (Fig. 3), no principled method for choosing NG (8 gates for 18 tasks), no ablation on gating strategy or learned task clustering
Inference latency increase of 10.7% (0.394s → 0.436s) not discussed for time-sensitive manipulation; dynamic viewpoint selection overhead during execution not measured

Missing technical details: (1) how ground-truth camera poses obtained during MVEP training, (2) no comparison with end-to-end joint training, (3) cross-attention implementation in TaskMoE not specified, (4) reward weight sensitivity analysis absent
Overstated claims: 'significantly outperforms' for modest 1.7% improvement; several tasks show negligible gains (+4%); real-world comparison limited to single baseline

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Figure 1 clearly illustrates genuine limitations of fixed-view systems (occlusion, incomplete scene understanding)
Comprehensive simulation evaluation: 18 RLBench tasks with ablations, sensitivity analyses, data efficiency studies, and zero-shot generalization testing
Dual complementary technical contributions: Active view planning addresses occlusion; TaskMoE addresses task interference—reasonable design combination
Real-world validation: Physical robot experiments on Dobot Nova demonstrate practical applicability beyond simulation
Thorough documentation: Detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and supplementary materials support reproducibility efforts
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Combines established techniques (MoE for multi-task learning, active view planning, cross-attention) without fundamental innovation. TaskMoE is incremental engineering rather than methodological advance
Modest empirical improvements: Only 1.7% gain over ARP+ (86.6% vs 84.9%); overlapping error bars on many tasks; no statistical significance tests reported despite claims of 'superior performance'
Inference latency penalty inadequately addressed: 10.7% increase (0.394→0.436s) dismissed as 'modest' despite importance for real-time control; no latency-accuracy trade-off analysis

Fundamental limitation inadequately resolved: Cannot handle transparent/reflective objects (acknowledged by authors). Real-world robustness testing (Table 7) shows poor performance under occlusion (90%) and illumination variation (30%), contradicting generalization claims
Limited real-world validation: Only 5 tasks with 10 trials each; robot system (6-DoF Dobot) differs from training environment (7-DoF Panda); insufficient scale for reliable conclusions
Complex three-stage training not justified: No ablation comparing full pipeline vs. end-to-end or two-stage alternatives. Necessity of Stage 3 unexplained. Reproducibility burden high

Pseudo-environment mechanism weakly validated: No ablation against actual environment interaction. Using frozen 'shadow network' may limit learning signal. Reward function (Eq. 9) sensitivity to learnable weights unexplored
Weak generalization claims: Zero-shot test uses single unseen task ('Open drawer') similar to training tasks. 12% success rate on OOD task contradicts 'generalization breakthrough' claims

Missing baselines: No comparison with other active perception or dynamic view selection methods for manipulation. Real-world comparison uses 2D baseline (Diffusion Policy) rather than 3D fixed-view baseline
Design choices unjustified: NG=8 gates, top-2 experts, reward component weights—all lack principled justification or sensitivity analysis
Statistical rigor lacking: No significance tests despite overlapping error bars. Overlapping standard deviations on several tasks (e.g., Close Jar: 100.0±0.0 vs 100.0±0.0)

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation with compelling visual examples demonstrating the limitations of fixed-view approaches
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including 18 RLBench tasks, 5 real-world tasks, thorough ablation studies, sensitivity analyses, zero-shot generalization testing, and data efficiency analysis
Strong empirical results with up to 56% improvement on occlusion-prone tasks and 88% real-world success rate vs 68% for baseline
Technically sound approach with clever pseudo-environment interaction mechanism (Algorithm 1) enabling efficient RL-based policy learning without expensive physical environment interaction
Well-presented paper with clear figures, thorough supplementary materials, and sufficient implementation details to support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: TaskMoE is a straightforward application of existing MoE ideas with cross-attention; MVEP is standard viewpoint selection RL; main contribution is engineering combination rather than fundamental innovation

Pseudo-environment mechanism creates potential circularity where dynamic views are selected to minimize losses from fixed-view model rather than for truly optimal views; lacks analysis of actual selected viewpoints and comparison to alternative reward formulations
TaskMoE contributes only 1.1% improvement (85.56% → 86.67%) while MVEP dominates with 77.8% contribution; zero-shot generalization validated on only single unseen task
Modest improvement over strongest baseline (1.7% vs ARP+), with only ~4% gains on non-occlusion tasks, limiting practical significance of added system complexity
Real-world validation limited to 5 tasks with 10 trials each and single baseline comparison; no comparison to other active perception or dynamic viewpoint methods
Incomplete justification for key design choices: why K=3, why top-2 experts, why NG=8 gates; learnable reward weights lack analysis; hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly explored beyond Table 3
10.7% inference time increase largely unanalyzed; no details on sampling acceleration and camera caching mechanisms; three-stage training on 4×A800 GPUs limits reproducibility
Point cloud quality assumptions; acknowledged limitation with reflective/transparent objects is non-trivial; no analysis of failure modes under degraded reconstruction
